assessment.nobel_worthiness: Opened a new observational window: a cubic-kilometre detector in Antarctic ice that detects high-energy astrophysical neutrinos, with the 2013 discovery of a diffuse flux and later source identifications (blazar TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068, the Galactic plane). It is a detector-driven discovery that created neutrino astronomy, which is the kind of result I value most.
assessment.attribution: Halzen conceived and led IceCube as the principal investigator, so the vision credit is clear, but the supplied credit is a single name for a very large collaboration. A prize needs the committee to decide whether other founders or instrument leads deserve recognition; I cannot resolve that from the longlist.
assessment.maturity: Diffuse flux confirmed by several independent analyses and channels, and source evidence has strengthened over a decade. Recognition now is timely; the source-population picture is still evolving but the discovery itself is secure.
uncertainties: Single credited name for a collaboration of hundreds; fair configuration needs expert review of who else was decisive.
Source associations (NGC 1068, Galactic plane) are recent and lean on a small number of events.
KM3NeT or Baikal-GVD have not yet independently confirmed the flux at comparable significance, to my knowledge.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The ATLAS and CMS detectors made the Higgs boson discovery possible at unprecedented rates and radiation levels. The physics was honoured in 2013, but the detector achievement is a distinct, very large instrument-building feat with lasting impact on the whole LHC programme.
assessment.attribution: Jenni (ATLAS), Della Negra and Virdee (CMS) are the recognised founding spokespeople and leaders of the detector concepts. This is a fair three-person configuration, though thousands contributed and some will argue for technical coordinators or accelerator leaders.
assessment.maturity: Both detectors have run for over a decade, repeatedly confirmed each other and produced a vast body of precision results. Fully mature, with some risk that the committee sees it as already covered by the 2013 prize.
uncertainties: Whether the Nobel statutes and committee practice favour recognising an instrument construction after the physics prize was already awarded.
Collaboration-wide credit makes any three-person selection contestable.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Measurement of the last unknown mixing angle theta-13 by reactor antineutrino disappearance, which showed it is large and opened the path to measuring leptonic CP violation and mass ordering. A clean, decisive and precise experimental result.
assessment.attribution: Daya Bay (Wang as spokesperson, Luk as co-spokesperson) and RENO (Kim) announced in 2012 within weeks of each other. The three credited names fit a fair split, but Double Chooz and the T2K appearance result also contributed and are not credited here.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by multiple reactors and accelerator experiments; the value is consistent across methods and has been refined to a few percent. Timely, especially after the 2015 neutrino-oscillation prize.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2015 prize on oscillations may reduce the committee's appetite.
Priority between the Daya Bay, RENO and Double Chooz teams, and the accelerator hints, needs careful weighing.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magnetars link a theoretical prediction of ultra-strong magnetic fields in neutron stars to observed soft gamma repeaters and anomalous X-ray pulsars, and their giant flares. It established a new class of compact object and ties to fast radio bursts.
assessment.attribution: Duncan and Thompson made the 1992 prediction; Kouveliotou led the observational identification of the field strength through the spin-down of SGR 1806-20 and SGR 1900+14 in 1998. The theory plus observation pairing is natural, although Paczynski and others had related earlier ideas.
assessment.maturity: Decades of confirmation across X-ray and gamma-ray missions, including the Galactic magnetar flare linked to an FRB in 2020. Mature and stable, though the longest-standing questions concern the origin of the fields.
uncertainties: Earlier or parallel proposals for strongly magnetised neutron stars could complicate the priority claim.
I am relying on memory for the exact history of the 1998 measurements.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: WMAP produced full-sky microwave maps that pinned down the age, composition and geometry of the universe and established precision cosmology with the standard LCDM model. A landmark measurement built on careful calibration and systematics control.
assessment.attribution: Bennett was the PI, Page led instrument and analysis aspects and Spergel the cosmological interpretation. The configuration is sensible, but WMAP was a large team effort and the Planck contributors might also be argued for.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed and superseded by Planck, so the results are very secure. Because cosmology prizes were given in 2006 (COBE) and 2019, the committee may judge the CMB area as already covered.
uncertainties: Overlap with earlier CMB and cosmology recognition (2006, 2019).
Planck's improvement may shift credit away from WMAP.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks with magic-wavelength trapping reached 10^-18 fractional uncertainty, redefining precision measurement and enabling tests of relativity, gravitational redshift measurement at the millimetre scale and the prospect of a new SI second.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed and demonstrated the magic-wavelength lattice clock; Ye built the highest-performing strontium lattice clocks. A two-person prize looks natural, though others such as Hall, Hänsch and ion-clock groups were already honoured or may be viewed as related.
assessment.maturity: Independently reproduced in many labs and compared across continents; the technology is mature and being adopted for redefinition of the second. Timely.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes in frequency metrology and ion clocks.
I rely on colleagues for the atomic-physics priority details.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution gave a physically secure method for key exchange, with real satellite and fibre implementations. It joins fundamental quantum theory to a concrete application, and strongly connects to the cryptography uses I often point to.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard's BB84 protocol is the standard invention credit; Ekert's entanglement-based E91 is an independent route that complicates a three-person prize and also a two-person one. Experimental pioneers are not in the credited names, so credit sits on the theory side.
assessment.maturity: Commercial and satellite systems exist and the protocols are well verified. However, practical security of implementations remains a subject of ongoing work.
uncertainties: Whether Ekert should be included or an experimental demonstration recognised alongside.
This is outside my own expertise; I defer to colleagues in quantum information.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical detection and coherent control of single NV centres in diamond turned a solid-state defect into a room-temperature quantum sensor and qubit platform, with applications in magnetometry, nanoscale NMR and biology. It is a precision-measurement tool that opened new measurements.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup and Jelezko demonstrated single-NV detection and control in 1997 and 2004; Lukin's group contributed key quantum-network and sensing advances. The configuration is plausible but Lukin's role may be seen as broader than NV centres.
assessment.maturity: Widely reproduced across many groups and already in applications, though many sensing applications are still developing.
uncertainties: Condensed-matter and quantum-information priority details are outside my own expertise.
Whether Lukin's contributions are decisive for NV centres versus other platforms.
